The implementation used the Randomized Hadamard Transform, which suits CPUs well because Hadamard matrices contain only +1 and -1 values, avoiding floating-point multiplication in the rotation step. The one-sentence heuristic: measure your KV-cache share of total GPU memory first, and if it is under 20%, TurboQuant is not your lever, no matter how good the paper is. results.title: TurboQuant: the new(?) and controversial ground breaking compression breakthrough from Google
results.content: The key-value (KV) cache is the memory structure that allows transformer models to “remember” everything they’ve seen in a conversation or document during inference. Without it, the model would have to reprocess the entire context from scratch on every token generation step. The problem is architectural and unforgiving: KV cache memory grows linearly with both sequence length and batch size, which means serving real users at scale pushes it past comfortable limits fast. [...] TurboQuant’s core mechanism applies quantization to KV cache tensors during inference, compressing the floating-point representations from 16-bit (BF16 or FP16) down to as low as 3 bits per value. The “Turbo” in the name refers to a novel transform applied to the KV cache tensors before quantization, the authors argue this transform smooths the distribution of values, making them more amenable to aggressive compression without the rounding errors that normally cause quality degradation. [...] To make this concrete, consider a 70B parameter model serving 100 concurrent requests at a 32,000-token context window. At standard BF16 precision, the KV cache alone can consume well over 100GB of GPU memory, potentially more than the model weights themselves. That’s not a theoretical edge case; that’s a Tuesday afternoon for anyone running a serious inference cluster.

results.title: What Is Google TurboQuant Compression Algorithm? How Does It Affect the AI Memory Chip Industry?
results.content:
TurboQuant is a new vector compression algorithm officially released by Google Research in March 2026, targeting the core pain point in the inference phase of large language models (LLMs) and vector search engines—the excessive memory consumption of the Key-Value Cache (KV Cache). Technical details will be formally released and peer-reviewed as an academic paper at ICLR 2026 (International Conference on Learning Representations) from April 23 to 27. [...] Google's TurboQuant algorithm significantly compresses AI inference memory, reducing Key-Value Cache (KV Cache) occupancy by up to 6x and boosting computational efficiency up to 8x on H100 GPUs, with minimal precision loss. While targeting inference, it's unlikely to impact HBM or NAND Flash demand directly. The technology could lower AI operational costs, enabling new use cases and driving exponential growth in total AI demand, paradoxically increasing overall memory requirements. Challenges [...] Industry consensus indicates that the current bottleneck for large models is not the number of parameters but memory capacity. The longer the context, the larger the memory footprint of the KV Cache, which eventually hits hardware limits before the model parameters do. This is a shared pain point for tasks such as long-text generation and long-document understanding.

TurboQuant's breakthrough directly addresses this pain point.

results.title: TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate
results.content:
We also provide a formal proof of the information-theoretic lower bounds on best achievable distortion rate by any vector quantizer, demonstrating that TurboQuant closely matches these bounds, differing only by a small constant (≈2.7\approx 2.7) factor.
Experimental results validate our theoretical findings, showing that for KV cache quantization, we achieve absolute quality neutrality with 3.5 bits per channel and marginal quality degradation with 2.5 bits per channel. [...] Existing VQ algorithms present a trade-off: either they lack accelerator (vectorization) compatibility and exhibit slow computation, making them unsuitable for real-time AI applications like KV cache quantization, or they suffer from suboptimal distortion bounds relative to bit-width.
Our objective is to introduce an algorithm that addresses these limitations. [...] For comparison, we benchmark our approach against several state-of-the-art memory-efficient methods, including PolarQuant , SnapKV , PyramidKV , and KIVI . Each method is tested under a memory compression ratio of 0.25, meaning that only 25% of the full KV cache is utilized.
